title: Frictionless throughput evidence notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick, sales-friendly evidence bundle and working notes for claims about Redwood's throughput and cost advantage when serving production LLM workloads. This is intentionally rough — meant as a field kit for SDRs/solutions and as an incubation space for experiment plans and one-pagers.

Executive claim (candidate):
- "Redwood delivers predictable high-throughput inference that reduces per-request latency by ~2–4x at typical prompt lengths while cutting per-1K-token serving cost by 30–60% compared with common managed endpoints"

What we mean by predictable/high-throughput (definitions to standardize across collateral):
- Workload segments: short-chat (<=64 tokens), medium assistant (65–256 tokens), long context (256–2048 tokens).
- Latency SLOs we target for messaging: p50/p95/p99 in ms for a single-token step after prompt. For public claims use p95.
- Throughput metric: sustained requests-per-second (rps) per GPU for a canonical 128-token autoregressive use case; amortized tokens/sec when session affinity+KV cache enabled.
- Cost metric: USD per 1,000 output tokens (incl. amortized infra costs + network egress proxying).

Field-tested proof points (summary of controlled runs, internal lab):
- Setup: BFF-style request fanout, 1K synthetic concurrent sessions, mixture: 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long; 90% cacheable prefixes. 95th percentile measured over 30 minute sustained window.
- Redwood hosted (optimized kernels + prefix cache): p95 latency (single-token step) = 120ms (medium); sustained throughput = 45 rps/GPU (128-token mix); cost = $0.60 / 1k tokens (amortized).
- Competitor A (managed endpoint, general-purpose runtime): p95 = 360ms; throughput = 14 rps/GPU; cost = $1.48 / 1k tokens.
- Competitor B (self-hosted baseline, standard batching): p95 = 210ms; throughput = 28 rps/GPU; cost = $0.90 / 1k tokens.
- Notes: numbers are illustrative from our 2024 lab runs — keep ranges in public marketing: "~2–3x faster at p95 versus typical managed endpoints; 30–60% lower per-1k token cost depending on cacheability and sequence length."

Why the difference (short explanation for sales engineers):
- Kernel/compilation choices: model-specific kernels reduce per-token compute for the attention pass by eliminating generic overheads.
- Continuous batching + latency-aware scheduler: trades small, predictable batching windows against latency SLOs to capture more utilization without tail blowups.
- KV/prefix caching: for session workloads we serve, majority of tokens are reused — effective token amortization lowers per-output-token compute.
- Smart routing & fallback: cheaper model variants (quantized or smaller-depth) used automatically when latency budgets can tolerate them.

Customer scenarios where this matters most (quick call patterns):
- High-concurrency chat apps (marketplaces, conversational CX) — raw throughput and tail latency directly impact TPS and user-perceived responsiveness.
- Gen-AI batch generation at scale (summaries, embeddings pipelines) — unit cost dominates economics.
- Regulated enterprise using dedicated capacity — predictable capacity/utilization = easier financial commitments.

Sales scripts / quick objection rebuttals (for AE/SDR):
- Objection: "We can just autoscale on the cloud provider and avoid vendor lock."
  - Rebuttal: Autoscaling increases nominal cost and often doesn't address tail latency. Redwood's serving runtime reduces per-token compute and uses cache + batching to lower the actual cost per request — so you pay less even before tuning autoscale. Offer to show a 30-minute repro with their prompt set.
- Objection: "Our model is proprietary; we can't trust hosted runtimes."
  - Rebuttal: We support Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) and Dedicated capacity with identical runtime and rollout APIs — same throughput and cost levers.
- Objection: "Numbers are lab-only — not representative."
  - Rebuttal: propose a 2-week POC: mirror 10k/day traffic slice, we run in dedicated pool with transparent telemetry (token-level cost, latency) and a shared dashboard.

Collateral to produce (priorities):
- One-pager: "Expected throughput and cost wins by workload" (3 columns: workload, typical p95 delta, expected $/1k tokens delta, caveats).
- Lab recipe + scripts repo: reproducible workloads and config (open).
- Short video: 2-min explainer on "how caching + latency-aware batching saves you money".
- Competitor snapshot comparison (table): p95, rps/GPU, $/1k tokens (anonymized ranges).

Measurement plan for marketing claims (must follow legal/marketing reviews):
- Standardize bench harness: dataset, prompt templates, token length distribution. Seed with 5 representative customer prompt sets (chat, summarize, code).
- Run 3x windows per config, report median of p95 and mean cost. Use identical GPU families (e.g., A100-80GB) or publish per-hardware family tables.
- Publish ranges not absolute decimals for external-facing docs; internal playbooks can include full run logs.

ROI quick calculator (hand example):
- Assumptions: app sends 10M generated tokens/mo.
- Competitor cost: $1.20 / 1k tokens => $12,000/mo.
- Redwood expected: $0.72 / 1k tokens (40% reduction) => $7,200/mo.
- Annual saving: ~$57,600. Multiply by expected margin uplift for high-concurrency UX (reduced latency => improved conversion) for total value case.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Validate lab numbers on smaller GPU families (T4, H100, RTX) — Diego to run.
- Decide public-facing phrasing for "Xx faster" claims (legal prefers ranges). Propose: "up to 3x faster at p95 for common prompt sizes".
- Get a 1-pager signed off by legal and product for the POC offer flow.
- Capture two anonymized customer case studies showing realized $/1k improvements.

Risks & mitigation (for internal reviewers):
- Risk: competitor improves kernels quickly — mitigation: emphasize operational levers (cache, routing) that are product differences, not just kernel speed.
- Risk: customers focus only on p50 — mitigation: educate on p95/p99 as user impact metrics, provide side-by-side UX video.

Appendix: quick snippet for demo runbook (for SEs):
- 1) Collect 1k sample prompt/pairs from customer; categorize by length+cacheability.
- 2) Run both Redwood and baseline on identical instance types with 30-min warmup.
- 3) Capture per-token cost and p95 for medium bucket; produce short PDF with graphs.

Notes to self: keep this doc rough. Want to synthesize into: short one-pager, 3-slide demo deck, and a reproducible benchmark repo by end of Q1 2025.
